utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yesterday I had finished responding on ground 1 of the appellant's appeal. This morning I would like to deal with a few points which had arisen from his arguments yesterday which concerned ground 2 of his appeal, and specifically, Your Honours, I'm speaking to issues he raised yesterday appearing on transcript pages 63 and 77. And essentially he argued he took issue with the Trial Chamber's admission of documents bearing Mr. Stakic's signature, which the handwriting expert had given his opinion on that they were possibly or probability signed by Mr. Stakic. And he took objection to their admission and in particular he referred to -- he made an example when the Trial Chamber had relied in paragraph 387 to one particular document which Mr. Stakic had signed. I think the reference given by the appellant yesterday was to Exhibit 288. Exhibit 288 is in fact the handwriting report; the exhibit which he's referring to in paragraph 387 is Exhibit number 64. So we will be dealing with that as well. He took issue with the standard being applied in a criminal trial. He said hat "possibly" and "probably" had no place in a criminal procedure. And, finally, in response to a question posed by Your Honour Judge Meron, when Your Honour asked whether he had objected at trial, he said that he had objected and in fact he had been denied then the opportunity to bring in his own handwriting expert. So I'll be dealing with all of those points. In our submission, the Trial Chamber did not err by relying on the documents bearing Stakic's signature, which the handwriting expert, Mr. Ten Camp, had opined had been possibly or probably signed by Stakic. Indeed, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber in the judgement paragraph 14 said that it was especially cautious -- I'll paraphrase what it says in that paragraph. The Trial Chamber said it was especially cautious when dealing with documents attributable to Mr. Stakic, requiring corroborating evidence from an expert and/or convincing witness testimony. And that's exactly what it did. Firstly, the signed documents - and it's important to note, to stress this - the signed documents were only part of the evidence, not the sole basis for the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraphs 336 to 408, some 20 pages of findings, very voluminous findings, about the Crisis Staff and Stakic's position and various roles in Prijedor, and particularly the Crisis Staff and the other bodies that he played a leading role in and in coordinating the three arms, the civilian, the police, the military, and regarding his role on -- in relation to the detention centres. Apart from this -- these documents of which Mr. Ten Camp, the expert appointed by the registrar upon the request of the Trial Chamber, apart from these documents, and there were some 15 to 20 that -- I'm approximating, but these were the documents signed by Stakic with which Ten Camp had given his opinion on, there was much other evidence which the Trial Chamber used in making these very important findings in paragraphs 336 to 408. In particular, there were a number other of documents such as Official Gazettes, newspaper reports, Stakic's own interviews in which he was asked questions; for example, in Exhibit -- the interview with the British television, Exhibit 187, in which Stakic was speaking and reflecting back on the period of the events and speaking of the level of cooperation between the civilian, the military, and the police. Also, not to forget, the evidence that was heard by the Trial Chamber from three Crisis Staff members, Budimir, Kuruzovic, and Travar. It was also the testimony of ECMM officers. In our submission, when -- the appellant is incorrect when he says the Trial Chamber must apply a beyond reasonable doubt standard to each document before admitting or relying upon it. It's a matter of weight to be given to each of these documents by the Trial Chamber, and this standard which he poses, beyond reasonable doubt, is a standard that applies to the ultimate findings, the ultimate finding of guilt or on essential elements of the crime or fulfilment of the elements of the mode of liability. Secondly, Your Honours -- [Trial Chamber confers with Legal Officer].

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, there was no error in the Trial Chamber having relied upon his qualified Dutch handwriting expert's opinions. His evidence, I point Your Honours, it's quite voluminous, it runs some 70 pages from transcript page 7459 to 7519. The fact that his opinions were couched in terms of "possibly" or "probably" was a matter that the Trial Chamber was fully aware of and could factor in when it weighed them. And this -- yesterday the appellant made the observation about paragraph 387, and in particular commenting on a document 64, Exhibit 64, which they noted that the Trial Chamber had in that paragraph noted that Stakic had possibly signed the decision. And, Your Honours, we would say that if you look at the paragraph, the italics, the fact that the word "possibly" is italicised to us highlights the fact that the Trial Chamber was particularly aware that the degree of certainty that the handwriting expert could give on this document was "possibly." So in fact it shows that they were fully aware that this was a matter to be given to the weight when examining this document in light of all of the other documents. And on this particular document, it's one which the Crisis Staff, where it demonstrated its ability to make decisions, it was an order concerning decisions on the release or continuing detention of certain prisoners, detainees, in the camps. And I think this shows the fallacy of the appellant's argument because the findings about Stakic's role in the detention centres or what he was able to do to contribute and to play a role in relation to the coordination and the setting up and the operation and maintenance of the detention centres, it doesn't rise or fall upon a single document. It doesn't rise or fall on document -- Exhibit number 64. In fact, this would be to ignore rely all of the evidence relied upon in paragraphs 377 to 401 of the judgement which was used to found his role in the detention -- in relation to the detention camps. I'd like to also address on his submission yesterday in response to Judge Meron's question when he submitted that they had objected to the documents and had actually taken issue and asked for their own handwriting expert. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not in error in denying his request for his own handwriting expert. In view of the fact that this expert was requested by the Trial Chamber and appointed by the registrar, he was a neutral expert, in our submission it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to only allow a second handwriting expert if it could be shown he possessed superior knowledge or expertise or methods of working. That was the test set out in its decision on the 8th of October. What has to be recalled: This was not a case where one side was allowed to call a handwriting expert and the other was not. The Trial Chamber called this handwriting expert. So having done that, it was then entitled to say that a second would not be called unless the Defence could show why one was needed. And the Defence could not and did not demonstrate this need. He didn't elaborate on this yesterday, but he does in his brief. It's all very well to come now on the appeal and tell us in quite some detail about the handwriting expert's proposed testimony, but when this matter was litigated, and the issue of experts was litigated some four or five times during the trial, but when it was litigated most extensively on the 25th of November, 2002, the Defence had no report and save for saying that the expert -- they wanted to call an expert called Mr. Hayes, save for saying that Mr. Hayes could testify about different international standards for verifying signatures, there was nothing else. This appears at transcript 9417. And in our submission, appeals are not the time to make up for what may be called trial tactic -- deficits in trial tactics. Nor, in our submission, can he show error simply by saying that the Dutch institute, the NFI, from whence, from where Mr. Ten Camp came from, that they used -- they prefer to use the two experts to verify signatures. Contrary to what he said yesterday, Mr. Ten Camp acknowledged different standards, different international standards, for handwriting analysis, but he did not say that you must have two. And importantly, neither in his brief nor yesterday, he has not, he's still not shown, how another handwriting expert's opinions would have led to a different result. So we ask Your Honours to dismiss his arguments relating to the documents, and in particular the handwriting expert. Your Honours, there are the only points I'll address you on in relation to ground 2. We've dealt at length in our brief, chapter 3, responding to the other arguments that he's raised in relation to the alleged procedural errors. In our submission, in short, none of those have substance. He has not shown either error or how it caused an unfair trial or how it would have led to a different result. If Your Honours have any questions on any of those issues raised in ground 2, I'd be more than happy to respond to those questions. If not, I will very briefly turn to ground 6, which is sentence.

Your Honours, that brings me to a close on grounds 1 and 2 and 6. I would now turn to my colleague, Mr. Mark McKeon, who will address you on ground 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Before I turn to ground 3, I wanted to just answer one question that was -- point of information that, Mr. President, you asked for about the Nuremberg reference that we made in our presentation. The citation to that, we referred to the judgement first of all and that appears in page 67 of the judgement. And then we also referred to the closing argument of one of the prosecutors, and that appears in volume 19 of the Nuremberg trial proceedings. It occurred on day 188, which was Saturday, the 27th of July, 1946, and was at page 496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the third ground of appeal, Dr. Stakic claims the Trial Chamber reached the unreasonable conclusion that he knew crimes were being committed in the detention camps and on the convoys. He does not in this ground of appeal challenge that he had knowledge that murders took place in the municipalities. Thus, even if this ground of appeal were accepted - and of course it's our submission that it should not be - the factual finding that he knew crimes were being committed in the municipalities would be undisturbed. Under this same ground of appeal, Dr. Stakic also claims the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he agreed to the consolidation of Serbian control in Prijedor in order to achieve the common goal of separating Serbs from "the other two national communities." In my presentation on this ground of appeal this morning, I will address first the standard of review for Dr. Stakic's arguments; and then secondly, I will address in the order that he's raised them his claims about the detention camps, the convoys, and then the goal of ethnic cleansing. I think it's important first of all to note at the outset that Dr. Stakic is not challenging in this ground of appeal any of the individual findings of fact, just the final conclusions to be drawn from those findings of fact. He accepts the individual findings of fact made by the Trial Chamber in this ground of appeal. And this is clear from the heading of his argument on page 40 that "the Trial Chamber's own factual findings undermine the inferences it drew in order to find that Stakic possessed the mens rea and the knowledge necessary to find him guilty on Counts 4, 5, and 6." If you look at the way his brief is structured, he recounts the findings that supported the conclusion of the Trial Chamber, then he lists the findings that he submits supported an additional or a different conclusion and argues from those other findings. What this also means is that the arguments made yesterday about claimed problems with individual pieces of evidence are not in large measure relevant to this particular ground of appeal, except for one or two exceptions which I will address, these arguments are not presented in the appeal brief and were raised for the first time yesterday. So in addition to the problems identified by Ms. Brady with these submissions, including the failure to identify the ground of appeal, the failure to identify how it caused a miscarriage of justice or which ground of appeal it applied to or even in many cases the failure to identify what in a particular paragraph was erroneous, it is also at this hour an unwarranted attempt to expand his grounds of appeal. Now, it's Dr. Stakic's position that based on the Trial Chamber's own findings of fact it should not have concluded that he possessed the mens rea and knowledge necessary to find him guilty on Counts 4, extermination, 5, persecution, and 6, murder. The standard of review for this type of review is whether any reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion the Trial Chamber reached from the factual findings it made. As this Appeals Chamber sitting for the Rwanda Tribunal recently raised in paragraph 241 of the Kamuhanda decision: "If the inference drawn from the evidence is a possible one, that inference is accepted on appeal." Thus, Dr. Stakic's arguments where he essentially replays his closing submissions from trial and tries to tell a different story from the one accepted by the Trial Chamber misses the mark. This is not a trial de novo. The standard is not whether a reasonable trier of fact could have accepted the conclusions now suggested by Dr. Stakic, but whether a reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusions actually reached by the Trial Chamber. The fact that a different reasonable Trial Chamber, or even this Appeals Chamber sitting as an original trier of fact, might have come to a different conclusion on the same evidence is not sufficient to meet the standard of review on appeal. I'd like to turn first to the camp killings. The Trial Chamber concluded that Dr. Stakic was fully aware that mass killings were being committed in the detention camps he himself assisted in setting up, and that the conditions in these camps of which he was also aware were likely to result in death, torture, and other forms of physical and mental violence against the detainees. That's in paragraph 838 of the judgement. The factual allegations that support this final conclusion of fact are summarised on page 40 through 42 of Dr. Stakic's opening brief and on pages 37 to 38 of our brief. And I will just mention those very briefly because they are summarised in our brief. This was based on evidence that Stakic was first of all permanently together with representatives of the police and military. And during those times together was a reasonable inference that they would have discussed the development of their common goals. This is in the judgement paragraphs 184 and 489. The Trial Chamber also found it of value that Stakic was aware of the conditions in similar detention camps in Croatia and in Bosnia where Serbs were being detained. He knew the conditions in those camps set up in the municipality of Prijedor would not be different from those established in other parts of Yugoslavia. It's in the judgement paragraph 596. He was informed about deaths in the camp, paragraph 597 of the judgement, and some deaths had been reported to him by Drljaca, paragraphs 375 and 392 of the judgement. He knew the camps existed, paragraph 400. He had agreed to the establishment of the camps and indeed signed order for the provision of supplies to the camps, paragraph 595. He knew there were discriminatory detentions in the camp, paragraph 401. And finally, the Trial Chamber found that the co-perpetrators, including Stakic, planned to consolidate Serbian power in the municipality at any cost, paragraph 591. The only reasonable conclusion to reach is that somebody who pursues the aim to consolidate power at all costs is aware that killings would in all likelihood occur and that he reconciled himself to that and made peace with the probable outcome. It was also relevant to the Trial Chamber that in light of Dr. Stakic's high rank he would have become aware at some point that killings and mistreatments were commonplace within the camps, especially Omarska and Keraterm, paragraph 596. And finally, Stakic was told by some witnesses about relatives detained within the camps, and almost all of them stated that knowledge of killings and mistreatment in the camps was widespread in Prijedor and yet Dr. Stakic did not intervene. In addition to these factual findings highlighted in the judgement, there are indeed other factual findings in the judgement that relate to his knowledge of killings. First of all, the Trial Chamber found in general that Stakic ensured that members of the police, army, and irregular forces were allowed to operate in a climate of total impunity. That's paragraph 615. Stakic was aware that this climate of impunity would in all likelihood result in killings. The existence of the camps was common knowledge among the Crisis Staff, as was the knowledge of the massacre in Room 3. That comes from the testimony of Mr. Kuruzovic in the trial judgement paragraph 394. Stakic knew the fate of his predecessor, president of the municipality, and many other well-known individuals were killed, paragraph 184 of the judgement. It's quite important that the Crisis Staff not only established these camps but also helped run them. The Crisis Staff coordinated security for the camps, paragraphs 381 to 384. The Crisis Staff made decisions about continuing detentions of people at the camps, paragraphs 386 and 387. The Crisis Staff controlled the food supply at the camps, which was found by the Trial Chamber to be grossly inadequate, paragraph 388. Paragraph 389, the judgement found that the Crisis Staff had indeed management and oversight functions in relation to the camps. And finally, and this relates also to the convoy findings, the Crisis Staff was responsible for organising transportation to and from the camps, paragraph 697. These factual findings show that knowledge of the killings and the mistreatment in the camps was widespread in Prijedor. The Trial Chamber was right to conclude from all of this evidence, and it had to view all of the evidence together, that Dr. Stakic as the highest civilian political figure in Prijedor, a man who was in regular contact with his co-perpetrators who were running these camps and who was involved with the Crisis Staff in the running of these camps, knew at least what everyone else in Prijedor knew. The Trial Chamber was right to conclude that it was inconceivable that these crimes could have taken place without the president of the municipality knowing about it. In addition, Dr. Stakic as the head of the civilian government made no efforts that we're aware of to ensure that the perpetrators were brought to justice or that at the very least an investigation was conducted. He did nothing to discourage further crimes in the camps and he made not one public acknowledgment of the crimes. His lack of any reaction to these crimes is evidence that he didn't care and that he in fact intended that these crimes took place as they did. Now, in his brief, Dr. Stakic points to other factual findings which he says suggest a different conclusion, that he didn't know about these killings. First of all, of course, the question is whether the factual findings that the Trial Chamber relied on supports its conclusion, and if you find that it did you don't need to consider whether other evidence might have supported a different conclusion; that's not the standard of review. I would note, however, as pointed out in our response brief that these factual findings that he has highlighted in his brief do not in fact support the conclusion that he urges. He doesn't identify very many of them and I can go through them very quickly. First of all, he says medical services were not conducted in Prijedor in a discriminatory manner; that in his brief at page 218. Well, that in fact is relevant to the issue of his knowledge of killings and does not undermine the finding of his discriminatory intent. He also points out that there were findings that the camps were under the control of police and military, but that does not mean that Dr. Stakic as the highest civilian authority didn't play an active role in setting up and running the camps, as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 400. Or, that he corroborated with the military and police leaders and used the Crisis Staff to support these leaders. There was some discussion in the brief and also yesterday about Exhibit S107, which was the order establishing the camp. Dr. Stakic made the point in his brief and as he did yesterday that this order had a paragraph in it which said that there must be secrecy maintained about what took place in the camps and that there could be severe punishments for anyone who broke these rules of secrecy. The interesting thing about this, though, is that this order of secrecy shows on the fourth page that the first copy of it was delivered to the Crisis Staff. It also refers on the first page that this order was issued in accordance with the decisions of the Crisis Staff. Therefore, the suggestion that this order somehow implies that Drljaca was unable to give information to the Crisis Staff about what was taking place at the camps, it simply doesn't support that inference. Moreover, the fact that the Crisis Staff received this shows that the Crisis Staff at least was aware that when the camps were being established, they were being established in an atmosphere of secrecy, in an atmosphere where it was important not to let people know what was going on at those camps. If anything, that is additional evidence that Dr. Stakic knew that killings and mistreatment were likely to take place at these camps. Mention is made in the brief that Dr. Stakic never visited the camps. That, in our submission, is irrelevant. His knowledge was not based on any information gained during a personal visit. The Trial Chamber didn't rely on that. He relies in his brief on the fact stated in the judgement that Dr. -- sorry, that Drljaca complained about the civilian leadership interfering in the work of the police and claims that this shows Dr. Stakic was uninvolved or uninformed; in fact, we submit that shows just the opposite. It shows that the civilian leadership, which included Dr. Stakic, were attempting to exercise such control over the police that they "attempted to transform the police into a council body which would execute orders given by the council civil authorities." And finally, Dr. Stakic mentions that there was a legal purpose that was put out to the world for these camps, that they were prisoners of war camp, interrogation. The fact that the authorities stated a purpose for the camps that they believed might be accepted by the outside world is meaningless when examining the question of whether they knew of the crimes being committed in the camps. Turning next to the convoy killings. The Trial Chamber concluded that Dr. Stakic was fully aware that mass killings and other persecutorial acts were likely to be committed by members of the Serb police and military forces during the convoys of detainees organised by the civilian authorities in Prijedor. That's at paragraph 824. First of all, as we noted in our brief - I think it was under ground 5 - it was not necessary for the Trial Chamber to categorise the killings into separate groups as they did or attempt to impute Dr. Stakic's knowledge for each category. The killings on the convoys were so related to the activities in the detention centre that there was no need for the Trial Chamber to establish Dr. Stakic's independent knowledge of this variety of killing. It's not critical to determine Dr. Stakic's liability for killing, whether the detainees were killed inside the camps or outside the camps. Secondly, general factors that apply to all of the killings also apply to the convoy killings. For example, the Trial Chamber found that Stakic ensured that members of the police, army, and irregular forces were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. allowed to operate in a climate of total impunity, paragraph 615, and that Stakic was aware that this climate of impunity would in all likelihood result in killings. That finding goes across the board. It relates to not only camps, not only municipalities, and not only convoys; it relates to all the killings. The Trial Chamber found that Dr. Stakic knew of the killings nevertheless, even though it's our submission it didn't need to go to that level, during the organised convoys, in paragraph 601. It found that Dr. Stakic took an active role in organising the massive displacement, paragraph 601, 377, and 697. It found that Dr. Stakic was aware that members of the intervention platoon were entrusted with taking some of those transports, paragraph 600. It found that the convoy that eventually became the Mount Vlasic massacre may have been in fact specifically discussed with Dr. Stakic. Indeed the tragic results of this convoy were so well-known in Prijedor that it beggar's belief to suggest that the head of the civilian authority in Prijedor who was actively arranged in convoys didn't know about it. Now, one of the challenges that we had yesterday was to this statement that the discussion -- that the convoy may have been discussed with Dr. Vlasic [sic] by Mr. Kuruzovic, and that reference was to paragraph 601 of the judgement. The argument was made that because Slobodan Kuruzovic only said that he may have discussed this convoy with Dr. Stakic, that this was not of a sufficient level to raise it to where it could be considered by the Trial Chamber. It's our submission, however, that this only goes, as with the other evidence that Ms. Brady discussed, to the weight of the evidence. It's clear that the Trial Chamber knew exactly what it was talking about because it did not in any fashion overstate Mr. Kuruzovic's evidence. In fact, there's no claim that it did. It says right in the judgement that he only said he may have discussed this. Secondly, the fact that he may have discussed it, as we mentioned, goes to the weight and could be weighed with all the other evidence that supports their conclusion. And finally it's important to focus on what it used this finding for. In paragraph 601 it found that the accused's knowledge of criminal acts is also proven by the evidence that he took an active role in the organisation of the massive displacements of the non-Serb population. To support that conclusion, it's not necessary to conclude that Dr. Stakic discussed the Mount Vlasic convoy itself with anyone in particular. What was important was that Dr. Kuruzovic indicated that it was possible that on this very convoy he discussed it with Dr. Stakic, which indicates that it was his practice to discuss convoys and that Dr. Stakic was involved in the displacement. There's other evidence, in fact it's not the only evidence in the record of that, about his involvement in the convoys, but it certainly is a piece of evidence that can be used to support this finding. Finally, I'd like to turn to the third error that they allege, the plan for ethnic cleansing. Dr. Stakic challenges the conclusions in paragraphs 469 to 471 concerning the plan to establish a Serb-dominated and Serb-controlled territory on the municipality level. In our response brief, we deal with the challenges Dr. Stakic raises to the Trial Chamber reliance on the so-called Variant A and B plan and on Karadzic's expression of the six strategic goals. It is important to note that the Trial Chamber was citing these two pieces of evidence because they most clearly expressed the content of the plan. The existence of the plan, however, is not shown only by these two pieces of evidence, but by everything that happened in Prijedor thereafter that followed the blueprint set out by these plans. The Trial Chamber spent over 80 pages of the judgement summarising these events, starting with the build-up towards the takeover of power in Prijedor, starting at paragraph 5 of the judgement. It described the takeover on the 29th of April on paragraph 67 through 84. It described the fate of the prominent non-Serb residents in Prijedor after the takeover in pages 172 and 184 and the propaganda campaign maintained against the prominent non-Serbs in paragraph 105. It discussed the commencement of the armed attacks against the non-Serb civilian populations on paragraphs 129 through 158. It talked about the establishment of the notorious detention centres immediately after these attacks in paragraphs 159 to 171 and it talked about the convoys of non-Serbs being driven out of Prijedor in paragraph 314 to 334. Your Honour, it's our submission that the existence of the plan is shown not only by the documentary evidence of its content but by the actions that showed that this blueprint was being followed. Your Honour, I have some additional comments to make on some of the questions posed by the Trial Chamber -- I'm sorry, by the Appeals Chamber. I don't think they relate to ground 3. So I can either go on to that or I can pause here if you have questions on the third ground of appeal.

utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, at line 41 you said it's not critical to determine Dr. Stakic's liability for the killings whether the detainees were killed inside the camps or outside the camps. Now, you mentioned the word "critical." Do you take your submission as high as to say that it's not relevant to determine that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always difficult to say that something is not completely irrelevant, but I think the point to keep in mind is that the question is whether Dr. Stakic was aware that killings could take place and he was aware that the people who were likely to commit these killings on the convoys were the very same people who were likely to commit these killings in the camps. And indeed, the victims were also identical. The victims on many of the convoys were from the camps. They were killed being taken from the camps. So we have an identity of perpetrator and we have an identity of victim. Therefore, we would say that it is only perhaps of marginal relevance that the killings in the convoys took place outside the gates of the camp rather than inside in terms of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, your argument is focussed primarily on knowledge by Mr. Stakic or awareness. What can you tell us on the basis of your argument this morning about evidence for Mr. Stakic's intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber found that he had -- as for the deportation and persecution -- I'm not sure of the thrust of your question. But it found that he had met the standard of intent for deportation and persecution because he in fact was responsible for helping to organise those events. And it found, based on all of this information that we have given you this morning and in the judgement, that he was aware of the substantial likelihood that killings would take place and thus had intent on a dolus eventualis standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So in the dolus eventualis sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: There are various statements made by the trial court in the sections to which you have referred, citing statements or comments contemporaneously made by Mr. Stakic suggesting that there should be no mistreatment of other ethnic groups in the camps, et cetera, that they should be well-treated. How do you explain these? This was the liberator attempt at that time, to build a barrier of deniability?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I think that's certainly an appropriate inference and it's the one the Trial Chamber drew, and I think it's open for the Trial Chamber to draw that from the evidence. It is not -- it is not unusual for people that are perpetrating crimes to offer public explanations, that they are men or women of peace and that all they want is peace. I think the Trial Chamber was completely within its rights as the trier of fact to discount those public statements, to give them little weight, and to look at what actually happened to determine his true intent. And I think that was appropriate on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: How different was -- since your argument is based primarily on awareness or knowledge, how different was the role and the responsibility of Mr. Stakic in comparison to other members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Well, the other members of the Crisis Staff included police and -- for example, Mr. Drljaca was I believe -- hold on, let me check here. Yes, Mr. Drljaca was a member of the Crisis Staff, attended Crisis Staff meetings. Mr. Drljaca certainly had direct control over the police, and there's no question about that, that Dr. Stakic had a different role than Mr. Drljaca. The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So Mr. Drljaca's responsibility would be sort of more prominent, wouldn't it? He also was involved in the orders to establish the camps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have to look at the fact that the Trial Chamber found in order to -- under the mode of liability it applied, it had to find that Dr. Stakic played a key role. And without playing a key role, which is greater than merely a contribution which is required under joint criminal enterprise, a key role, that was the only way it was willing, the Trial Chamber, to find him liable. So everybody -- and under this theory of liability, everybody has their part to play. He was not the military leader. He was not the police leader. But without a civilian leader who was willing to do what Dr. Stakic did, this plan would not have worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: How would you compare his responsibility to other civilian persons or personalities who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff. He was also, as indicated, on the three -- or in the judgement of the- all three bodies that were involved in coordinating actions. He described himself in an interview that's cited in the judgement at one point as I believe the mayor of Prijedor. I think in terms of a civilian authority you could not find someone with higher civilian authority than Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Any of my colleagues? And if not, you can continue. You can go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to address your first question, but I'm not sure if this is the appropriate time to do it or if it should be done later, because I think we would need to go for a brief period of time into private session because I can't really address your first question, which involves testimony that was given in closed session, in open court. It would be very difficult to do. So I'm prepared to do that now if we -- if you would -- if we could go into closed session or private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will go into a closed session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We are in open session, and I will ask my distinguished colleague, Judge Pocar, to ask his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry to come back to, but before perhaps the Prosecution moves to another subject matter I would like to ask for a point of clarification. In dealing with the factual situation that you dealt with until now, you pointed out that the standard to be applied is that if the inference from the evidence is a possible one, that inference should be accepted on appeal; if I'm correct, you used more or less these words. But would you agree with me -- just a clarification I'm asking from you. Would you agree with me that more correctly the standard to be applied would be that if the inference from the evidence is one that a reasonable trier of fact could have reached beyond a reasonable doubt is the standard to be applied, this should be accepted on appeal. I wanted just to make sure whether you -- your point is that the Appeals Chamber should stick to its constant standard applied, or if you are suggesting a different standard of review when considering alleged factual errors?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity you've given me to clarify that. No, I'm not suggesting that there be a different standard. In fact, what I was attempting to emphasise is that there is no different standard for different types of evidence. It's sometimes been suggested that there is a different standard for circumstantial evidence, and it is in fact the standard you stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. This clarifies the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You still have -- you can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd now like to turn to the questions that -- the other questions that you've asked us to comment on. First of all, question 5, which is the mode of liability question that asks for both parties: "If the appellant's responsibility were to be analysed in terms of joint criminal enterprise, JCE, would the elements of JCE be fulfilled based on the findings of the Trial Chamber?" It was also a question for the appellant, it was not asked of us, but: "Would the appellant still have objections to the reliance of the consent of dolus eventualis within the framework of JCE and, if so, what would be the basis for such objections?" Your Honour, we've given a great deal of thought to how we should -- or how we could respond to this question. And our problem in determining what sort of information we can give to assist you on this is that we're having trouble identifying which ground of appeal this relates to. Dr. Stakic has not challenged the mode of liability used by the Trial Chamber and we certainly haven't challenged it; and thus, since there's no challenge to the mode of liability, we can see no basis for substituting one mode of liability for the one used by the Trial Chamber based on the grounds of appeal raised by the parties. Thus, any answer we gave or attempted to give would be in the abstract without knowing what the claimed error is, where the problem is, and how the answer might solve the problem because we don't know what the claimed problem is. A second problem that we have, Your Honour, is that if this is an issue that's not being raised by the parties but is instead something that the Chamber is raising proprio motu, we are not prepared to give a full and complete response in the summary fashion that we would be required to do so in the midst of a short oral argument where we would only have a few minutes to address it. If this is something that relates to the basis of the conviction or somehow affects the sentence, Your Honour, with all due respect, it's our submission that it shouldn't be decided by the Appeals Chamber except after full briefing and argumentation by the parties. We would like to be able to assist and to help the Chamber get answers to the questions it has, but it is difficult to do that in such a short period of time. As you know, for example, the elements of joint criminal enterprise are quite complicated. As you're aware, I believe, two aspects of the joint criminal enterprise mode of liability are presently on appeal in the Brdjanin case; they're being raised there. The issues are so significant and important that the Appeals Chamber even asked in that case that amicus briefs be filed by the Association of Defence Counsel. So it's difficult to respond briefly in an area where in addition to the other problems the elements of the mode of liability are uncertain and are before this Chamber in another case. In fact, one of the issues that's involved in the Brdjanin case is an issue that would perhaps cause discussion here, which is whether the physical perpetrator needed to be in the JCE; that's an issue in the Brdjanin case. We submit in the Brdjanin case that the theory of indirect perpetration used in Stakic applies both to JCE and to the theory used in Stakic, but that's still a question that's before this Court. In addition, Your Honour, the problem that we have is that the Trial Chamber itself didn't analyse the evidence on a joint criminal enterprise theory, and thus, trying to take the findings from the Trial Chamber and to put them into joint criminal enterprise becomes sort of like trying to take a square peg and putting it into a round hole. They didn't necessarily make findings on the things that could be relevant for joint criminal enterprise liability because they didn't need to. For example, there are findings in the judgement on Dr. Stakic's intent but except for some implications that you might be able to get in deportation not on intent of the other members of the joint criminal enterprise. Just because there's no finding on that doesn't mean that based on the evidence there could be findings, it just means that the Trial Chamber didn't make findings because it was not relevant to their analysis. It doesn't mean that there's not evidence to support that. If you were to try to find the missing findings now, that, in our opinion, because you're challenging the whole -- or going against the whole basis of the judgement, would require a review of the entire record, not just the findings of the Trial Chamber. And it would involve a re-writing of the entire judgement. And frankly, Your Honour, there's no challenge that we're aware of from the Defence to the current mode of liability that would necessitate such a review and re-writing. In addition, Your Honour, as we thought about this question, we're unable to identify from the question what it is that the Appeals Chamber might think is deficient in the judgement now that would require it sua sponte to analyse the evidence under a JCE theory. If there was an opportunity for proper briefing of this question, our position might be in fact that there's no error in the judgement and no need to analyse the case under a joint criminal enterprise theory, but we don't have an opportunity to present that because we don't know what the problem is that this is supposed to solve. And finally, after reviewing the argument given yesterday by Dr. Stakic's team, it's even difficult to see what issues we're responding to from the Defence side. I think their basic answer to the question: Is there sufficient evidence? Can be summed up to saying: No, there's not. And other than saying: Yes, there is, it's difficult to know how to respond to that because there's not particular legal issues that we're responding to. So, Your Honour, if we're to go into this in more full detail and this is something the Chamber is pursuing, we would ask that it be done in the appropriate manner, which in our view would be to have briefings from the Defence indicating what the issue is that this goes to so that we have something that we can respond to. Now, Your Honour, with all those caveats and disclaimers, I'd like to give a limited response to the Chamber's question as best I can, recognising that there's going to be many issues that we're not going to be able to go into. First of all, it was our position at trial that the evidence - not the findings but the evidence - was sufficient to sustain a conviction on a JCE theory. That evidence is summarised in detail and can be found at pages 42 through 66 of the Prosecution's final trial brief, and we would refer to the evidence discussed there that would support this theory of liability. As to the findings of the Trial Chamber, it's also our position that some of these findings can easily be translated into terms of joint criminal enterprise. For example, as to the acts reus, co-perpetration requires an agreement to reach a common goal by coordinated cooperation and joint control over the criminal conduct. This is actually more than is required by joint criminal enterprise. Joint criminal enterprise does not require joint control over the criminal conduct. Joint criminal enterprise also does not require that an accused play a key role, as is required for this mode of liability, only that he plays -- has some role. Also we would submit, there's no real substantive difference between an agreement to reach a common goal by criminal conduct, as was used in the judgement, and the JCE requirement of a common plan involving the commission of a crime. Thus it would be our submission that the fact that the accused met the higher requirements for co-perpetration means that on those issues he would also meet them for joint criminal enterprise. As to the mental requirement for JCE, the Trial Chamber found that the accused and his co-perpetrators acted in the awareness that crimes would occur as a direct consequence of their pursuit of the common goal. Now, if you translate that to joint criminal enterprise terms, for joint criminal enterprise there needs to be an agreement to commit at least one crime. They have to share the intent, the mens rea. There is no explicit finding on the mens rea of members of the criminal enterprise because it was not required. It was only required that they prove the mens rea of Dr. Stakic. But what they did find, for example, on deportation at paragraph 710 it said: "The evidence has established the close and coordinated cooperation between the civilian authorities led by the accused, the SJB, and the military authorities." This proves, we submit, that the appellant's conduct in the political field would -- his intent was shared by other members of the JCE, at least in the area and the crime of deportation. At paragraph 712 they found that the accused intended to deport Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the non-Serb population from Prijedor municipality, and at least in terms of joint criminal enterprise 1 if you find that there is a shared intent to commit at least one crime between the accused and other members of the joint criminal enterprise, you've proven it. You then go to a joint criminal enterprise 3 theory to see with the remaining areas where there has been no findings, and what we have is essentially that Dr. Stakic had an awareness of the reasonable likelihood that additional crimes could take place, it's our submission that as with the acts reus part of it on the mental element this is actually greater that has to be proven better JCE 3. So at least on these elements that we've discussed I think that there would be no problem translating those findings from the theory used in the judgement into joint criminal enterprise language. Finally, if I could just briefly address the question that was posed by President Meron yesterday asking us to identify the most egregious evidence demonstrating the involvement of Dr. Stakic in the joint criminal enterprise as well as his relevant intent and knowledge. First of all, we're interpreting that question where it says joint criminal enterprise with a small "j," a small "c," and a small "e," meaning the criminal enterprise, not some technical sense a joint criminal enterprise. But I tried to think in the brief time I had last night how I could convey the evidence to the Appeals Chamber because the record in this case is quite voluminous. This doesn't ask for the findings, it asks for the evidence. I think the statistics are that there were 108 witnesses who testified viva voce and under Rule 92 bis, 15.000 pages of trial transcript, and approximately 1448 exhibits, and I'm a bit reluctant to point to any one piece of that evidence as the key piece of evidence, particularly given the Blaskic standard that if there is a re-review of the evidence, you are essentially going to look at the evidence that we point you to and not at the whole record. I think that's what Blaskic suggests. So I'm reluctant to identify any specific parts because I don't want to limit the review, if we go there, to those specific parts. I think the best place, though, to get a look at the key evidence out of all of this that we selected ourselves as being the key evidence is in the Prosecution's final trial brief. This is, as you know, a case based on circumstantial evidence, and when it's a circumstantial -- largely circumstantial evidence, we also have direct testimony and documents. But when you look at that and you try and look at all the evidence as a whole, it's difficult to say which piece is important. It's like if you're building a puzzle and you're trying to say which piece of the puzzle is the most important to the picture. There is no piece that is the most important. It's all together and all must be considered together, both on the acts and the knowledge. But certainly from the trial brief you could see on the acts front, you could see information about Stakic's rise to power in paragraphs 7 to 11; the importance of the Municipal Assembly and the National Defence Council, paragraphs 12 to 14; the critical role of the Crisis Staff, paragraphs 15 to 20; Stakic's role as president of the Crisis Staff, paragraphs 21 to 25; his role within the SDS, paragraphs 26 to 29; his public role in concealing crimes, paragraphs 66 to 7; and then finally, the ways that Stakic used his power and influence, including his role in the Prijedor coup, his role in the detention camps, his direction in support of the police and the military and his role in the propaganda campaign. If there's a section which is probably key, it's probably that one. And that's on paragraphs 29 to 65 of our final trial brief. On the knowledge issue, in addition to the evidence that I've highlighted this morning, I would direct your attention to paragraphs 71 to 77 of your final trial brief which discusses his knowledge of crimes and paragraphs 78 to 86 which discusses the particular pieces of evidence that shows that crimes were organised and were intended by Dr. Stakic. I think, Your Honour, that concludes what I have to say unless there are any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You still have a few minutes to continue, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm done, but my colleagues aren't, so I'll turn over the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, I understood you to be dealing with a question as to whether the case evidentially considered could be accommodated under the JCE theory. And my impression is that your answer was in the affirmative. Did you have in mind any particular category of the JCE theory, such as the third category perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that our theory at trial and as set out in the final trial brief is that the evidence supports putting all of the crimes under JCE 1 and that as an alternative basis that crimes could be put, some of them, under JCE 3, if there was a JCE 1 crime proven. The answer might be one way if we had to look at the findings of the Trial Chamber because they simply didn't make findings on this, and it might be a different answer if you were to examine all the evidence, as we submit would be the proper way to analyse it. And it's our position from the final trial brief and it's our position now that the evidence would support this is a JCE 1 case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We will now go on to 10.45 and then have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be responding to the alleged errors with regard to Article 3 of the Statute. I will today address only the alleged legal error concerning the standard of the mens rea for murder. In respect of the other alleged errors, I would like to refer Your Honours back to our response brief, paragraph 6.2 and following. The Trial Chamber relied for the conviction of Dr. Stakic for having committed murder under Article 3 of the Statute on dolus eventualis. The appellant alleges that the Trial Chamber thereby committed an error of law. He argues that dolus eventualis is not sufficient to constitute the mens rea standard for murder, rather, according to him, murder requires purpose in the sense of aiming at or, as you referred to, the conscious object to kill. Our position in the response brief is that the mens rea for murder does not require purpose in the sense of aiming at the death of the victim, rather, we have set out that our position is that the mens rea for murder is met when the accused is aware of the possibility that death is going to occur as a consequence of his conduct and willingly takes that risk or is indifferent towards it. Since the arguments in support of this are set out in our response brief, I will not repeat them today. Rather, I will focus on the question whether the conviction for murder stands, taking into account the factual findings made by the Trial Chamber and considering the jurisprudence rendered by this Tribunal since the filing of our response brief. It is our position that the conviction for murder stands because, first of all, the recent case law which I will address in a minute supports that purpose in the sense of aiming at the death of the victim is not required. On the facts of this case, the requirements for the mens rea for murder are met, regardless of whether they require the awareness of a possibility that that was going to occur, as we have set out in our response brief, or whether they require the awareness of a higher likelihood, a substantial likelihood, as suggested by the recent case law. The conclusion with regard to the factual findings for murder under Article 3 are found in paragraph 616 of the trial judgement. And I would like to quote from paragraph 616: "Dr. Stakic, in his various positions, acted in the knowledge that the existence of such an environment would in all likelihood result in killings and that he reconciled himself to and made peace with this probable outcome." Therefore, the Trial Chamber found two elements. It found that Dr. Stakic acted in the awareness of a high risk in all likelihood that killings would occur, and it found a volitional element of reconciling himself with or making peace with that outcome. I will now address the recent jurisprudence which supports, in our submission, that purpose in the sense of aiming at the death is not required, and rather the awareness of a substantial likelihood is sufficient. The case law of this Tribunal, as we have set out in our response brief, considers intention to kill as sufficient to establish the mens rea for murder. The Appeals Chamber in the Dragan Nikolic case indicia in paragraph 39 accepts that this intention to kill is not limited to purpose, rather, it is possible that an accused - and I'm going to quote from paragraph 39 of the Dragan Nikolic appeals judgement - that the "accused forms the intention to kill either directly or with the awareness of the substantial likelihood that the victim would be killed." A similar interpretation has been used by the Strugar Trial Chamber with regard to the mens rea for murder. The Strugar Trial Chamber in paragraph 235 said that: "The mens rea for murder is not confined to cases where the accused acts with direct intent." In paragraph 236, the Strugar Trial Chamber says, and I quote again: "The necessary mental state exists when the accused knows that it is probable that his act or omission will cause death." Both the Appeals Chamber in the Dragan Nikolic case and the Trial Chamber in the Strugar case relied for their finding that awareness of a substantial likelihood is sufficient under Blaskic appeal judgement and the Dragan Nikolic case, also in the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement. The Blaskic and Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement found that in addition to direct intent the awareness of a substantial likelihood is sufficient to constitute the mens rea for the modes of liability of ordering. And the Kordic and Cerkez appeal judgement confirmed that also for planning and instigating. Although these findings were made with regard to modes of liability, they are, in our submission, applicable to the mens rea standard for the crime of murder because the national law referred to in the Blaskic appeal judgement, in order to reach that standard of awareness of substantial likelihood, is not national law with regard to the mode of liability of ordering, rather, it is national law which addresses the general mens rea standard for crimes including murder. Regarding the volitional element, the making peace with or reconciling oneself with, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber found in paragraph 41 that in addition to the awareness of a high risk, a volitional element must be incorporated in the legal standard. But it stated in paragraph 42 that acting with such an awareness, that is the awareness of a substantial likelihood, has to be regarded as accepting that crime. Therefore, once the awareness of a substantial likelihood is proven, the additional volitional element is proven as well. To conclude, the recent jurisprudence supports our view that purpose in the sense of aiming at the death of the victim is not required, and regardless of whether the standard for mens rea is the awareness of a possibility, as we have set out in our brief, plus willingly taken the risk of being indifferent to it, or whether there is, as is suggested by the recent case law, the awareness of a substantial likelihood, it is met on the facts of this case because, I quote again from paragraph 616 of the Trial Chamber judgement: "Dr. Stakic, in his various positions, acted in the knowledge that the existence of such an environment would in all likelihood result in killings." Therefore, the conviction for murder under Article 3 stands and the ground of appeal should be dismissed. This ends my submissions, and I'm available for Your Honours' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Goy. We have no questions. We will -- we still have nearly 15 minutes to the break, so I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. And then I will pass over to my colleague, Mr. Tracol, who will address you on the alleged errors regarding Article 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall now provide the response of the Prosecution to the fourth ground of appeal of the Defence relating to crimes against humanity, but I shall also speak about the seventh ground of appeal of the Defence which relates to cumulative convictions. As regards the response of the Prosecution will be, I shall be rather brief concerning the seventh ground of appeal. For the fourth ground of appeal, I shall also be brief as regards extermination, and I will spend more time to answer the questions of the Appeals Chamber relating to deportation. Given that I don't have much time, may I suggest to the Appeals Chamber to provide a response of the Prosecution to the seventh ground of appeal, i.e., cumulative convictions, I shall be very brief. Then if I have some time left, I shall provide the response of the Prosecution as regards the fourth ground of appeal, crimes against humanity. And I shall start off with extermination. I shall begin with the response of the Prosecution to the seventh ground of appeal of the Defence relating to cumulative convictions. The Defence submits that none of the elements of extermination are materially distinct from persecutions. The Trial Chamber convicted Milomir Stakic for persecutions and for exterminations quite rightly in paragraph 842 of the judgement. These two crimes against humanity satisfy the test of materially distinct elements. Even though Stakic was convicted both for persecutions and exterminations based on the same facts, the Prosecution notes that a name in our judgement, the Trial Chamber of the ICTR also convicted three co-accused for persecutions and extermination also. I here refer to 1.088 to 1.094 of the Nahimana judgement. Persecutions and extermination both comprise one element that is materially distinct and that's not present in the other. Persecution compromised materially distinct elements from persecutions, i.e., persecutions require the proof of an act or omission which introduces a discriminatory effect and also that the act or omission was committed with the specific intent to discriminate. On the other hand, extermination compromises also elements which are materially distinct from persecutions. In the Kordic and Cerkez judgements, in paragraph 1.041 the Appeals Chamber held that murder requires the proof of the death of one of the people which is not required for persecution. The Appeals Chamber thus concluded that cumulative conviction for persecutions and murders is legitimate based on the same facts on Article 5 of the Statute. So extermination, what is extermination other than a mass murder? Extermination requires the proof of mass killings, which is Ntakirutimana judgement of the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR, paragraph 521, also the intention to kill on a large-scale. There I referred to the mens rea. The next paragraph of the Ntakirutimana judgement. Therefore, cumulative conviction for persecutions and extermination is legitimate based on the same facts under Article 5 of the Statute. I have concluded as regards the response of the Prosecution relating to the seventh ground of appeal of the Defence. I still have a few minutes left. Unless the Appeals Chamber would like to ask me any questions regarding this issue, I suggest moving on to the response of the Prosecution to the fourth ground of appeal of the Defence relating to crimes against humanity. As I mentioned, I shall briefly look into extermination before spending more time on the issue of deportation. As regards extermination, as far as its actus reus is concerned, the position of the accused is that the actus reus of extermination is mass murder and the position of the Prosecution, therefore, in line with the Ntakirutimana judgement in paragraph 521. Mass murder does not mean that there are thousands of victims contrary to the allegations of the Defence. In the Stakic judgement, paragraph 640, the Trial Chamber held that it is not - and I shall quote this paragraph - "necessary to set a minimum number of victims." The Prosecution fully agrees with this finding of the Trial Chamber, which is in line with the recent case law of the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, Brdjanin, paragraph 391 of the judgement; Blagojevic and Jokic, paragraph 573; in addition, the recent case law of the ICTR, Ntakirutimana judgement, paragraph 522; Gacumbitsi, paragraph 309; and Rutagnira, paragraph 49. As far as a mens rea element is concerned in the -- requires intent to kill, which is identical to mens rea in murder, but intent to kill on a large-scale which is distinct from extermination. Different from the Defence submits that the existence of the knowledge of a large collective murder plan and the participation of the accused to this large-scale project are part and parcel of the definition provided for extermination. The elements contained in extermination have been defined in the Brdjanin judgement and Blagojevic and Jokic judgement. These two judgements don't even mention the existence of knowledge of a large-scale collective murder plan. Conversely, the Trial Chamber concluded in paragraph 576 of the Blagojevic judgement and Jokic judgement that the Prosecution need not prove the existence of a large criminal enterprise. In addition, the recent case law of the ICTR confirms that a mass murder killing is the essential element in extermination. I once again refer to paragraph 521 of the Ntakirutimana judgement; paragraph 522 of the Gacumbitsi judgement, paragraph 309; Ndindabahizi, paragraph 479 and 480; paragraphs 49 in Rutagnira judgement. These four decisions never mention in this element the knowledge of a large mass murder collective plan. In the definition of extermination, this is why the Prosecution asks you to reject the ground of appeal relating to extermination presented by the Defence. Given the time, maybe the answer relating to deportation response provided by the Prosecution could be done after the break because I shall spend more time on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: That is I think reasonable, and we will now have a break and reconvene at 11.15 sharp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, you will now continue. You have -- the Prosecution has 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall now respond to the Defence's submission as regards deportation. As I mentioned a while ago, I shall attempt to provide a response to the Appeals Chamber regarding this particular issue. Now, as far as an actus reus is concerned, deportation and crossing of national borders, the Prosecution deems that deportation under Article 5D of the Statute includes not only illegal displacements inside and outside the national borders of a state, but also forced illegal displacement in a territory controlled by one party. The Prosecution appealed this point in the Martinovic/Naletilic case. Let me refer you to the appeals brief of the Prosecution of the 14th of July, 2003, paragraph 4.5 and following. This particular issue is still pending before the Appeals Chamber, as it is a ground of appeal presented by the Prosecution in the Naletilic/Martinovic case. The Prosecution admits that in light of the recent jurisprudence of the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal relating to the definition of the actus reus included in the deportation and forced transfer that these opinions, they are, to say the least, divergent. So the decision relating to the motion for acquittal in the Milosevic case decision rendered on the 16th of June, 2004, paragraph 68, the Trial Chamber considered that deportation and forced transfer differ in that deportation require cross-border -- or crossing, whereas forced transfer take place inside the national borders of a state. In the Brdjanin judgement, the Trial Chamber expressly referred to the Stakic judgement in paragraph 541 and clearly indicated that it disagreed with the position of the Trial Chamber in the following paragraphs in the Stakic judgement. Contrary to the definition applied by the Trial Chamber in the Stakic judgement, the Trial Chamber maintained the Brdjanin judgement, paragraph 542, that border crossing of a state is the factor distinguishing deportation from forced transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts. In the Brdjanin judgement, paragraph 543, the Trial Chamber concluded that deportation requires border crossing of a state, whereas forced transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts infer that the transfers take place inside the borders of a state in which are the victims. The actus reus of deportation is thus different from that of forced transfer as underlying acts to other inhumane acts. The Brdjanin judgement supports a position set out by the Prosecution in its brief in reply as the Trial Chamber concluded that national border crossing is not included in the definition of forced displacement and is thus therefore not an element of forced displacement as an underlying act to other inhumane acts. In the Brdjanin judgement the Trial Chamber, however, considered that deportation require border crossing of a national border which is not the position of the Prosecution. However, the Trial Chamber concluded in Blagojevic and Jokic judgement, paragraph 549, -- that customary international law punishes displacements inside or beyond the borders of a state because they are prohibited by international law, whether the people had been displaced beyond the national borders or not. In its order relating to the preparation of the appeals hearing dated 26th of September, 2005, the Appeals Chamber asked the Prosecution to clarify the following: Point 8 of this order. If for extraordinary reasons the Appeals Chamber held that the border crossing is an element of deportation, are we then talking about a de jure frontier, a de facto frontier, or a frontier generally recognised? The Prosecution notes that in the Krnojelac judgement, paragraph 218, which I shall now quote: "The Appeals Chamber holds that forced displacements placements, underlying acts in the crime of persecution and punishable under Article 5(h) of the Statute are not restricted to displacements beyond a national border." Alternatively, the position -- or the Prosecution feels that this should be a de jure frontier; in other words, a frontier that is internationally recognised as in the case of a peace agreement. The Prosecution, and I for one have read the transcripts of yesterday afternoon, from what I understood of the position of the Defence, the Defence is also in favour of a de jure border. In this case both parties disagree on every point, but there's one point which at long last is a point on which both parties agree. The Prosecution recognises the parties need clarification and instruction from the Appeals Chamber on this particular issue. In addition, the jurisprudence of the Trial Chambers -- the Trial Chambers do not apply the same jurisprudence. Now, so that everything is quite clear, the Prosecution is -- does not agree with the opinion provided by Judge Schomburg annexed in the Krnojelac judgement because Judge Schomburg felt that a de jure border was sufficient to state the case. However, whenever there is no crossing of a national border de jure, the Prosecution feels that forced transfer is an underlying act and part of other inhumane acts. Crossing of a border, if it is de facto, is therefore, according to the Prosecution, not an element of forced transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts. Let me stress once again that I'm talking about the position of the Prosecution here. Alternatively, it is in line with -- which is in line with the motion for acquittal which was filed in the Milosevic case on the 16th of June, 2004. Now, if we are to address the mens rea of deportation and the intent to permanently transfer the victims. The Defence admits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions regarding the legal elements of displacements and deportations that you explained. Judge Pocar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Maybe a point of clarification. I thought our point, according to the Prosecution, that it should be the de jure border. If I heard correctly, you said, Mr. Tracol, in other words, a frontier which is internationally recognised. Can you be more specific. What do you mean by that? Because there are three possibilities: A de jure border, a de facto border, a de facto internationally recognised. You mean only the de jure border, that of course is internationally recognised clearly, or what do you mean with your expression? If you could be more precise, that would help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I admit that I have perhaps been a little bit redundant when I referred to a de jure frontier because I would find it difficult to define a frontier other than by calling it de jure or internationally recognised. I just wanted to specify this and tell you what a de jure frontier definition is and what the Prosecution meant when it used this term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... de facto --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me thank you, Judge Pocar. Let me just pursue this a little bit. So, for the term "deportations," we need de jure crossing, crossing of a de jure frontier. You also say that forced displacements within a national territory might be criminal but it would be criminal under a different heading. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the main position of the Prosecution on this issue is as follows. Existence of a frontier is not an element of deportation nor of forced transfer. To try and answer the question put by the Appeals Chamber: If, nonetheless, the Appeals Chamber holds that crossing a frontier is required to establish an element of deportation, the position of the Prosecution alternatively is to say that it must be a de jure frontier. This being said, this does not include transfer with no crossing of a de jure border. For this kind of criminal conduct, according to the Prosecution, this should relate to forcible transfer and underlying acts and other inhumane acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol. [Interpretation] You claim that the essential position of the Prosecution is that for the definition of deportation a frontier is not requisite. We must -- if the Trial Chamber is of the view that to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. contrary a frontier is required, then the requirement must be a de jure frontier. Don't you think there's a contradiction in the position you hold? In other words, the position you have, do you think there's a contradiction here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't feel that there is a contradiction here. All the briefs that have been filed by the Prosecution, the Prosecution has always stated that the crossing of a border is not an element of deportation and of forcible transfer either. I shall not stand before you to state the contrary today. We maintain our position. But given that the Appeals Chamber has asked us a very clear-cut question, if the Appeals Chamber feels that crossing a border is an element of deportation, what kind of frontier are we then talking about? So alternatively, and this has nothing to do with the main position of the Prosecution, we suggest that we cross a frontier which is a de jure frontier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't challenge your position; that is not why I find there is a contradiction. But between your position and your position alternatively, is -- do you -- is -- do you say that a frontier, if it's a de facto frontier, would that be closer to your initial position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not necessarily, according to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. What we would like to find out is the following: Since the Prosecution is telling us that it is necessary to cross a border for deportation to be established, we would tend to think that you would make do with a de facto border rather than requiring a de jure border, which is something that is much more difficult to have, to establish, to define. Because for that purpose there are a number of rules that need to be met.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is not convinced that it is more difficult to prove the existence of a de jure border than of a de facto border and of the crossing of such a border. This question, needless to say, will have to be examined by Trial Chambers on a case-by-case basis. But according to us, we do not believe that the distinction between these two kinds of border is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but let's not talk about the evidence now. Don't you think that your main position when you say that it is not necessary to cross a border for deportation to be established, don't you believe that this will not lead us to another proposition, i.e., if you believe that there needs to be a -- a border needs to be crossed, then it is not necessary to be a de jure border. I believe that's the point we would like to raise with you and we would like to have your comments about this point as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there is a border, there has to be a border, well, then, it should be a de jure border, then it's much clearer, according to the Prosecution. Once again, the Prosecution maintains its main position. I've covered the various jurisprudence sources from the Trial Chambers, and we acknowledge that the way the jurisprudence has developed is not quite favourable to the main position of the Prosecution. But we maintain that it is much clearer to have a de jure border as an element for deportation. It's much more clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But your -- thank you for your question to Judge Vaz -- for your answer to Judge Vaz. But your preferred position, if I understand it correctly, is that deportations within its meaning under the Statute could take place without regard to whether there are international borders or not, just forcible displacement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the main -- the thrust of the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... leaving aside some major difficulties which I, like Judge Pocar and Judge Vaz, saw with the de facto as well as the de jure problem, you note that we are always very much concerned as an institution that does justice with not violating the principle of sine lege. We are very conscious to the principle of legality. Now that's why we always take into account the customary law underpinnings of the Statute. Now, Article 49 of the Geneva Conventions which speaks of deportations has historically been interpreted as involving international boundaries.
