So when you say, Well, it's legal and important for the Prosecution, I would like some rationale for that, because we are not anxious to create new offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution has conducted some research in customary international law in order to determine whether in international customary law there are more elements pleading in favour of a de jure border rather than a de facto border. We have not found any legal basis to support the position in one way or the other. Therefore, the position we have taken is not based on any specific element of international law. But once again, I'd like to repeat that we've conducted -- we searched, tried to find if there was a legal basis one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I must say that I have a little bit of a problem with -- not with the notion of the de jure, assuming that we are -- that you also accept the de jure border approach, but then you are saying you must have -- if a border, it must be de jure, it must be de jure. So imagine there is a border which is -- there has been fighting between two territories for the last 10 or 15 years, there has been a demarcation line which has been recognised by the United Nations, by the Security Council, as something which creates a certain status and certain implications in terms of use of military force, so those -- and one of the countries expels a part of the population. So this still being formally de facto border, this is not a deportation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I apply the main position of the Prosecution, I would say that such a criminal conduct could be characterised as deportation or forcible transfer. By contrast, if I apply the alternative position of the Prosecution, i.e., the cross-border of the de jure border, then it would be an deportation. In any case, what is important for the Prosecution is that the criminal conduct of transferring civilians, this conduct has to be criminalised, whether it is an deportation or deportation when a border is crossed or a forcible transfer as an underlying act of other inhumane acts when there is -- when no border is crossed, when it is within the confines of a territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, thank you for -- Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, I understand you to be answering

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON THIS WAY
utterances.text: That taking the example he gave, you find that there is an act of deportation, not however because you consider that there is any virtue in there being a de facto border but because in the first instance you don't think there is any need to prove that there is any cross-border crossing at all, whether de jure or de facto. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the position, central position, of the Prosecution that we've developed in our briefs in the Stakic case, amongst other cases. Crossing a border, whether it be a de facto or de jure, is not an element of the crime of deportation or forcible transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Pocar or -- I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Just help me on one further point I should have been able to discern the answer myself. Regrettably I have to appeal to you. What then is the distinction which you make between forcible transfer and deportation if deportation does not require any cross-border crossing of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our position, both these crimes are equivalent. There's no specific distinction between deportation and forcible transfer from that point of view. By contrast, if the Appeals Chamber decided to use cross-border crossing, the crossing of a national border as an element of distinction between deportation and forcible transfer, then every time the border is crossed de jure, according to the Defence, or de facto according to the Prosecution, then we would be talking about deportation, whereas when there's no cross-border crossing we would be in the position of forcible transfer as an underlying act of other inhumane acts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Pocar or Judge Guney. Judge Guney, we'll start with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tracol, you said that after conducting research within the case law of the Tribunal you came to the conclusion that this was not in favour or this was contrary to the main position of the Prosecution. If I'm not mistaken, you also stated that after conducting some research within the corpus of customary international law, you were not in a position to find elements pleading in favour of one or the other position. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on I tried to review the resent jurisprudence of Trial Chambers in relation to the definition of forcible transfer and of the actus reus of that crime. A number of decisions have been rendered in the Milosevic case, in the Brdjanin judgement, in the Blagojevic and Jokic judgement as well. It's true that when you look at these decisions and the way the jurisprudence has developed, it's not in favour of the main position of the Prosecution where we say that the transfer of -- across a border, national, is not an element of forcible transfer. And we acknowledge that. It is true as well that as part of our research into international customary law before this hearing, in preparation of this hearing, in order to determine whether we could find elements in favour of the crossing of a de facto or de jure national border, we were not to find -- we were not able to find any elements for or against our position. Therefore, I don't think that this will help us to determine the position one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the outcome, whatever the outcome of the -- your research, you still maintain your position. But on what basis, on what basis do you maintain this position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first basis is the Krnojelac appeal judgement because the Appeals Chamber deemed that crossing a national border was not necessary to establish forcible transfer as an underlying act of deportation. Therefore, the Krnojelac appeals judgement has been relied upon by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's the only -- in the only appeals judgement you relied on because you told us that the research you conducted within the case law of the Tribunal goes against your own position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the case law of the Trial Chambers' decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Guney on a follow-up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Pocar, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tracol, I'm not going to dwell too much on the question I asked earlier on, but I'd like to come back to the answer you gave to Judge Shahabuddeen, probably based on the position you adopt which I understand it. It's not a matter of saying whether the position is correct or not, but I understand your position. In other words, the border itself is not one of the elements of the crime, but if that is the case, if the crossing of the border is not required, then there's still something I do not understand is why, if this element is required, then why would you prefer a de jure border and why don't you say that it could be either a de jure border, a de facto border, a recognised border? There would still be a border. It's part and parcel of your main position, according to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not necessarily. Because if you think that the crossing of a de facto border is not part of the forcible transfer as inhumane acts, in that case border crossing is not relevant to define forcible transfer as an underlying act of inhumane acts. In other words, and on the other hand, any crossing of national or de jure border would lead to establishing the crime of deportation. I do not believe that our alternative position is completely contradictory with our main position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you say is that the persons are displaced across a de facto border, then this could be characterised -- well, provided that the cross-border crossing is an element of crime, then in that case you would say that this could not be qualified as deportation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's exactly contrary to what you answered to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even realise that. I'd like to clarify the position of the Prosecution, it's our alternative position. But let me try to answer the question of the Appeals Chamber with regard to the actus reus. For us what is important is that any transfer of population committed by a defendant should be criminalised. The distinctive element between deportation and forcible transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts can be the crossing of a de jure border. If a border has been crossed, then we are talking about deportation; if it's not the case, we are talking about forcible transfers as an underlying act of inhumane acts, whether a border -- a de facto border has been crossed or not. This does not matter in the case of forcible transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... questions as far as we can and perhaps you should be allowed to continue, to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to answer as best I could, Your Honour. Now I'm going to deal with the mens rea of deportation and the intent to transfer victims on a permanent basis. The Defence submitted that the Trial Chamber found that the mens rea of deportation is that the perpetrator must have had, and here I quote paragraph 687 of the judgement: "The intent that the victim is removed which implies the aim that the person is not returning." In the Stakic judgement the Trial Chamber has not considered whether the accused had acted with the intent to transfer victims on a permanent basis. The Trial Chamber acknowledged at paragraph 687 of the judgement that if a victim were to return this would consequently not have any impact on the criminal responsibility of the perpetrator who removed the victim. As in the Stakic judgement, the Trial Chamber did not consider whether the accused had the intention to transfer the victims on a permanent basis in the Martinovic and Naletilic judgement. Permanent removal was mentioned both in the Martinovic/Naletilic and the Stakic case, but nevertheless a misunderstanding has arisen. Because these Trial Chambers seem to have concluded that permanent removal was an element of deportation. However, both these Trial Chambers have not applied these supposed legal findings to the facts of the case. As a consequence, they have not deemed permanent removal to be an element of deportation. The Prosecution has referred in its brief to the -- to a quote from the Martinovic/Naletilic judgement in order to illustrate the test for cumulative convictions in that respect, but I'm like to state that according to us the mens rea of deportation is limited to the intent to transfer the victim and that the intent to transfer the victim on a permanent basis is not required. Furthermore, we acknowledge that the recent case law of Trial Chambers related to the definition of mens rea of deportation is contradictory. In the decision and motion for judgement of acquittal rendered in the Milosevic case in the -- on 16th of June, 2004, the Trial Chamber did not rule that the mens rea for forcible transfer and mens rea for deportation require permanent removal of the victims. By contrast, in the Brdjanin judgement the Trial Chamber stated at paragraphs 545 that the Prosecution must prove the intent of the accused to displace victims on a permanent basis bore both for the mens rea of deportation and for the mens rea of forcible transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts. This contradictory position related to the mens rea of deportation and to the mens rea of forcible transfer as an underlying act to other inhumane acts adopted by the Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin judgement and by the Prosecution in its brief in response is linked to the diverging interpretation of the Martinovic/Naletilic judgement and namely of one of the sentences of this judgement at paragraph 520, let me quote it for you: "The intent of the perpetrator must be that the victim is removed which implies the aim that the person is not to return." In the Brdjanin trial judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that the Prosecution must prove that the accused intended for these displacements to be permanent. In our brief in response, we proved by contrast that this is not an element of deportation and of forcible displacement as an act underlying persecutions. The Prosecution appealed against the findings of the Trial Chamber related to mens rea of deportation and mens rea for forcible transfer as an underlying act to inhumane acts in the Brdjanin judgement. This is the fifth ground of appeal of the Prosecution, and I'd like to refer to you to pages 69 to 81 of our brief in the Brdjanin case. We maintain that the intent to displace the victims on a permanent basis is neither an element of the crime of deportation, neither an element of the crime of forcible transfer as an underlying -- inhumane acts. Indeed, if the intention to displace victims on a permanent basis was required, it would turn deportation and forcible transfer into a crime the element of which would be de dolus specialis,.as it is with genocide, persecutions and torture. An accused could only be deemed guilty for deportation and forced transfer if the Prosecution can demonstrate that there has been ethnic cleansing and, on the other hand, that the accused has proven his intent to take part in this cleansing. The Stakic case, the Trial Chamber has concluded that the Prijedor municipality has sustained ethnic cleansing, Stakic judgement paragraph 330, 331, and 704, and has also stated that Mr. Stakic did have the intent to take part in this cleansing, paragraph 706 of the judgement. This interpretation runs counter to this definition of deportation and forced transfer, i.e., Article 49 of the fourth Geneva Convention which you referred to earlier this morning, Your Honour. This provision clearly states in its first paragraph, which I shall now quote: "Forced transfer, whether it be mass or individual, as well as deportations are prohibited for whatever reason." To interpret, deportation and forced transfer as crimes containing a specific intent would run counter to their original meaning. In addition, the Statute, the case law of the Tribunal, and the authorities and matters of law provide no legal basis for that requirement, i.e., specific intent. The Statute and the conventions and treaties should foresee a specific intent. For instance, Article 4(2) of the Statute clearly sets out the special intent for genocide. However, the Statute does not provide a definition for the mens rea in case of torture. In the Forungia [phoen] judgement, the Appeals Chamber adopted those elements relating to torture set out in Article 1 of the United Nations Convention for Torture. And in paragraph 111, which I stated, the definition provided in Article 1 of the convention against torture is in accordance with international customary law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: We are -- I hope that you are nearing the end of your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because of your questions, but if you could finish in two, three, minutes, I much would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. We need to accept that the requirement of specific intent, i.e., that the victims do not return, are -- do -- are not a part of Article 5(d), (h), and (i) of the Statute. We need to look at international customary law to determine whether or not there is a reason to interpret deportation forced transfer as containing a specific intent. None of the text relating -- none of the legal text as regards deportation and forcible transfer, Article 4.9 of the fourth Geneva Convention, nor Article 6C of the Nuremberg charter mention any specific element. This is why the Prosecution asks you to dismiss this element. I could proceed, Your Honour, but as I only have three or four minutes left, I shall stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tracol. We will now turn to the Defence and you have 30 minutes for your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May it please the Court. My name is John Ostojic along with Branko Lukic, we're here on behalf of Milomir Stakic. Just briefly in connection with yesterday's questioning and request, I think the President asked other paragraphs with respect to common goal, and we were able to find yesterday quickly paragraph 553, but I'd like to direct your attention also to 475 and 479 of that -- of the trial judgements -- of the trial judgement, as well as 470 and 472 where they discuss at length. What I'd like today is talk a little bit about sentencing but also respond in kind to some of the issues that were raised or omitted to be raised by my learned colleagues at the Prosecution. I think it's fair to say hat I mentioned to the Court I wasn't going to discuss sentencing yesterday because I wanted to reserve the time today, and we did discuss what I considered to be some rather critical and important issues. By no means anything that we failed to discuss orally are we waiving or suggesting that we're abandoning that claim. We think that with respect to sentencing we raised some very critical issues, both on the issue of proportionality and as well as the aggravating factors that the trial court used in sentencing Mr. Stakic to what we consider to be an unduly harsh and a large sentence given the circumstances in other cases. The reply I thought would have been with a response, with all due respect, would have addressed some of the issues that we raised in our brief. It was silent on that. All they did as reiterate that there was a gravity of crime that they thought was significant and that they thought the sentence was sound. I disagree, respectfully, and I disagree that they should have accepted that because we didn't address it yesterday that we don't maintain our concerns. The six elements that the Trial Chamber looked at aggravating we believe are not only subsumed in the actual conviction, but we think that they shouldn't in and of itself be considered aggravating. So we have two positions on that, we'll discuss it hopefully later, but I'd like to discuss some other issues, if I may. I thought extermination was a critical element or a critical count, and I thought there was much to discuss about extermination. The Prosecution doesn't think so. We've raised, I think, although one of the Prosecutors, I believe, suggested that we don't have a problem with the mode of liability. I think from our discussion yesterday, I have a very serious problem with the mode of liability. I think the biggest problem and what I didn't hear an answer to is how on one hand can we have the trial court at paragraph 616, I believe, tell us affirmatively, in my view, and in my view again, rather unequivocally that they do not believe that Dr. Stakic had the conscious object to kill, yet on the other hand they convict him of murder which in their view requires a mental element to kill and they convict him of extermination, which likewise obviously one of the six elements requires an intent to kill. The Trial Chamber further discusses that it's necessary not to replace or to change the specific elements of a crime when we're using mode of liability. That presents yet another and different problem that we tried to discuss yesterday. If that's true, and we believe that it should be, that then you couldn't have both results. You can't have an unequivocal affirmative statement that Dr. Stakic does not have an intent to kill and then convict on specific crimes which ultimately require an intent to kill. I'm just a little surprised that we didn't have at least their position on that and to have some reconciliation as to what is it that their position might be. But perhaps, as I've heard in deportation, the discussion, their position may depend. It may depend on who asked the question, and it may depend on what facts they can take to answer the certain question. However, and in all seriousness, because I think they're very important issues, I think when we look at this trial judgement that we all agree that under the Blaskic test, and I know some of you respectfully dissented from that and have used it as a guilt determinative test, I think it's coined. But I think that honestly both sides see that this particular Trial Chamber erred in many ways, and this Trial Chamber failed to give a reasoned decision on many critical points, including the critical point of mens rea on deportation, as acknowledged by the Prosecution. Now, if I may, with respect to extermination we've set out what we think are the six critical elements, and we also argue that there should be a temporal scope that is more confined than what was suggested in the case -- in the underlying case below. We don't hear their answer on it, and I'm not sure if they agree or disagree on it. But I think for extermination that's one of our highlights in terms of what our position is, that there should be a temporal concept involved, and I think the definition in and of itself, not just the vast amount but the collective nature of the crime I think requires that it be done in a shorter, more confined period, subject to determination and evaluation, obviously, by the triers of fact. What I'd like to address now, before I go on to sentencing, is specifically our position on the whole as to the factual findings of the court. We believe that the Court erred in a lot of legal areas, and in some instances, the trial court, respectfully, was correct in the law yet applied the law incorrectly, as we've discussed. For example, we believe that they were correct to say you cannot replace elements of a crime by using mode of liability, yet they do that. We think they're wrong, the trial court, we think the trial court is wrong in the law when they suggest that in dubio pro reo should not be applied to legal construction and only applies to factual construction. We believe the Trial Chamber is wrong when they confuse the specific Article 4 requirement for special intent with that of persecutions, Article 5, discriminatory intent. We think there are a lot of errors. I know that the Prosecution -- I'm sure that they know that dolus specialis is not the same as discriminatory intent. I'm sure they don't want discriminatory intent to be raised to the level of dolus specialis, but perhaps they do, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because they want to increase the level of intent specifically as it may relate to persecutions to that of genocide. However, given those -- given those, what I consider to be legal errors, among others, I think that it's important that -- to note that we tried yesterday and we established in our briefs, we believe, that there were critical factual errors that the court erred. So what we're saying is the court erred in how it examined those facts and came to an unreasonable conclusion as to those facts, thereby applying unreasonable facts to whichever law they decided to select, we think is a miscarriage of justice. Now, the Prosecution at one point citing an ICTR case said that it should be a possible inference, and I believe that the Court corrected them and said that it should be a reasonable trier -- it should be a reasonable inference that's sought, not just the possible inference or something to that name. What we're saying is the Court erred in defining the facts, and we say they erred in finding the facts in numerous ways. One was that they misquoted -- they misunderstood. Two was that there was conflicting testimony. So when you balance the two facts, whether Dr. Stakic was somewhere or wasn't somewhere, that you couldn't but infer in his favour to say that he was not there. Those factual points, I think, are outlined in our brief, and we urge this Court, as did the Prosecution, if, respectfully, you do look at it under the standard of Blaskic, that you go over those facts I think with a little more scrutiny than perhaps the trial court did, if I may so suggest. What we also said is that there were many, many errors that the trial court made that affected the ultimate trial that was undertaken below and that in fact it -- Dr. Stakic did not receive a fair trial. I don't know exactly what the Prosecution's point was other than perhaps to say it's harmless error. Our position is that in some instances some of the errors that we highlight may be considered harmless error if taken in one isolated context. However, our position is quite clear, that the even harmless errors that the trial court below committed, when you cumulate them and the cumulative effect of those harmless errors equate to prejudice and a denial of a fundamental right such as having a clear and concise indictment, which is the first thing we wanted to discuss. It's interesting that the Prosecution suggests that the Court didn't rely on preparatory and post-indictment period in their trial judgement. We wholly disagree with them. Specifically, not only did they rely on it, it exacerbated the sentence that was given to Dr. Stakic. And what I'm referring to is specifically paragraph 917 - I believe - of the -- yes, of the trial judgement. Paragraph 917 clearly says that we took the long phase of preparation, which was ultimately everything before April 30th as well as the planning as an aggravating factor. So the Prosecution's position is somewhat odd. They're suggesting, well, he was charged only with the crimes here. What we're saying is that he was charged actually almost in a duplicative manner because they refused to amend the indictment, that being that he was charged for a crime that occurred from April to September of 1992, and because he was convicted of that crime now they're going to sentence him to a greater sentence because of preparatory conduct that we believe the Defence was never given an opportunity to address or rebut. The errors we suggest that the Trial Chamber made specifically relate to the manner in which they restricted our questioning, and I'll admit or be the first to admit that lawyers sometimes tend to go on for rather long periods without making a point. But my point is this: During the trial we believe that we should have had an equal opportunity to question witnesses on matters that they present if they were outside the scope of the indictment. We've shared with you what we thought were the transcript pages suggesting that the trial court failed or otherwise refused to give us that same equality of arms. The trial court below erred as a matter of law in denying Dr. Stakic's due process rights to have a fair trial. There was underscored. Underscored, I suggest, by the failure to give us the opportunity to call an expert to rebut or at least to clarify the issues relating to handwriting signatures. We suggest that there were seven or so multiple attempts to try to determine if the signatures were Dr. Stakic's or not. The expert that was called clearly stated that they have a standard that they use, which is not universally accepted. I have a problem with that, because this being an international court, and we discussing yesterday international criminal law, if we can use such arbitrary and perhaps inconsistent standards to determine a person's guilt based on the evidence similar to the arguments that I've made with dolus eventualis, you can't take a German standard and hope to apply it unless I believe it's universally accepted. In this instance Dr. Ten Camp decided that there was no standard greater than "possibly" for him. In his own article, he suggests to verify that my opinion is correct, you should always have a second forensic handwriting expert review the material in order to verify that in fact it is true and accurate. We ask the Court, pointing to that, the Court rejected. The Prosecution misses the point and suggests that all we did is identify an expert but we didn't submit the report. We don't have the resources, and we've never had the resources to get the expert, to pay the expert, to have him prepare the report in advance of it having authorised by the registry or the Tribunal. We wish we would have had the opportunity that any expert, and I would like to get names from anyone who can offer me that, an expert who was willing to do the work, prepare the report without being paid in advance. It's just impossible for us to have done that. We identified an expert who I made contact with, who agreed to examine it, in our view, to give an objective and independent review of that material, yet the trial court rejected our request on that. I think that caused Dr. Stakic a miscarriage of justice, and it was denied his due process rights to have a fair trial. Among other facts, among other findings that the Court made, we also suggest that there was a statement -- if I can just find it for one second. That there are various documents that suggest that Dr. Stakic was present at certain SDS meetings, which I think is part -- part of the -- what the Trial Chamber found. What the Trial Chamber found is that he was present in some. If we look at the evidence, which we hope that you do, and I'm suggesting that you follow this, only eight out of 30 meetings was Dr. Stakic in attendance at the SDS meetings, which is the political party, I'm sure as you know. But what we think is even more critical, not only that he was in less than ten, SK12, SK46, and SK47, forgive me, I couldn't find my notes on that. But what we think is significant is that when you go to your own political party's viewpoint, perhaps you would express your own feeling on the situation, and it is then that we think the most nationalistic-type speeches should logically be given to your own close, tight-knit group that you're purportedly opposing. In this instance, when Dr. Stakic was recorded as having or reported to have some conversations, he did not have any criminal intent. He did not share any of the discriminatory intent that is necessary for persecutions. He did not at any time say that there should be a permanent displacement of any ethnic group. All Dr. Stakic did was to try to tell everyone that peace must be maintained at all costs and that we should try to get the economy to start working again. That's the reality of the situation. His utterances within that time period were extraordinary, but they were extraordinary in proving his innocence, not his guilt. The only utterance or statement of Dr. Stakic that the Trial Chamber used was the one from 1993 where he did regrettably make that statement, for which he, I am sure and I know, greatly regrets making such a comment and truly doesn't believe that he would have even made that comment, but nonetheless he did. Whether it was an excited utterance or whether it was just misspeaking, he did make the comment. That alone, I suggest, should not, given the sentence given here, should not have any court, much less a Trial Chamber, find him guilty of the serious crimes that they've alleged occurred and of the serious crimes that he was ultimately convicted of. Just quickly, because we are running out of time, on extermination, another quick question that the Prosecution failed to recognise. If on one hand the Trial Chamber decides that the negative analysis approach is indeed something that should be rejected, why on the other then do they apply the negative analysis approach to extermination? Can they reconcile the two? They don't. Those two must be reconciled. We raise that in our brief in discussing not only the mens rea of extermination, but when we discuss actus reus in extermination because what the Trial Chamber did, and they use the word, negative approach, is acceptable in extermination in determining whether extermination has been met. In those cases, we believe that the trial court erred both factually and legally. And we believe the appellate court should re-review that and give us some sound guidance as to what the law truly is. Yesterday we did speak just quickly on this criminal enterprise issue and whether I was maybe -- I believe I was correct in stating that the evolution of it comes from common purpose and common design. And from that I think it just ultimately became joint criminal enterprise. I didn't hear an answer other than to say, well, we need to brief it because they're not sure. They're truly not sure what their position is on joint criminal enterprise. I was glad to hear that they think that joint criminal enterprise 1, the basic kind, is the kind that they believe this Trial Chamber found Dr. Stakic guilty of; that's not. And I must repeat, that's not what the trial judgement found. It's not even close to that. So in a way, they are also asking this Court, because they do mention Blaskic several times, to in fact re-review the entire trial transcript. The Trial Chamber did not find Dr. Stakic guilty as a principal perpetrator. They did not find Dr. Stakic guilty as a perpetrator. They did not find him guilty as a co-perpetrator as defined in other decisional authority. They did not find him guilty as a direct co-perpetrator. They found him guilty as an indirect co-perpetrator which is something that decisional authority hasn't addressed. I don't believe that the trial court ever found, other than on paragraph 16 [sic] where they say that there is a conscious object that he did not intend to kill, that they ever addressed his mental state specifically relating to the crimes and the charges against him. 616. 616, but I think we know. It says "16" on the transcript but ... Just quickly on Kvocka and what the evolution of joint criminal enterprise, if I can cite Kvocka and direct the Court's attention to 117. It states here: "Joint criminal enterprise requires existence of a common purpose." We've been talking about common -- then it goes on to say: "Which amounts to or involves the commission of a crime." Now, they cite some evidence to suggest or some paragraph to say that the Court found that the common purpose and the common objective was ethnic cleansing. It is absolutely not true. It is absolutely inaccurate. The Court did not find that the common purpose was ethnic cleansing. It did not. They don't cite any reference to it, and I dare say that I believe there is no such reference to it. The six factors -- and this is very important for Dr. Stakic because I've spent a lot of time in trying to -- in understanding this case, so I have to turn to sentencing, although I wish I could spend just a little more time on some of the issues hat they raise. They talk about Article 3 and 5, though they don't ever tell the Court -- and I think there was a question, was the mens rea ever discussed, was it decided, and then how do you reconcile it with the absolute statement that he did not have the intent to kill. What do they fall back on? The actus reus. They talk about knowledge and awareness. There's a huge difference between those two principles in my view. To have knowledge of something is different than to be aware of something. I think those principles need to be, quite frankly, with all due respect, clarified and some additional guidance perhaps is needed on those issues. With respect to substantial contribution and significant participation, that, too, needs perhaps some elements or guidance from the Court, if we can get it, on those issues. In this case, all they could do is to say that his title was such-and-such, therefore we can presume that he must have had significant or substantial contribution. Well, his title and his educational background apparently is what exacerbated his sentence. How do you, if you find someone guilty of committing murder, sentence him and then tell him that we're going to aggravate, we're going to find as an aggravating factor that you killed someone, that there's a death involved? Either you're going to find him guilty and not use that as an aggravating factor. All the aggravating factors that the Trial Chamber used are not aggravating factors, have never been recognised as aggravating factors, and I believe should be rejected as aggravating factors. The Court finds, for example, as an aggravating factor that Dr. Stakic was educated and is a physician. They try with that factor to try to apply the ICTR cases, and there's three of them on point that they cite, and they say those three cases doctors were involved, and they got sentences, and they were doctors and they got extremely high sentences as to suggest that the underlying crime that they were ultimately convicted of had no relevance. The underlying crime of all those three cases in the ICTR that the trial court cites, the underlying crime was genocide. One of the defendants got four counts of genocide against him, which in my view warranted a life sentence. In this case, we don't have genocide, and I believe -- I believe that we may not -- and I'm not trying to be deferential. I'm just suggesting in this case that we do not. So we're taking that as the view. And I believe that this Trial Chamber will find from the four arguments that they raised yesterday, three relating specifically to genocide, that the arguments absolutely should be rejected. Now, just because he's a doctor he should be punished more? Because we're lawyers or judges we should be held to a higher standard? That's the question really that I was hoping that the Prosecution would answer. Should we hold different individuals to higher standards? Similarly, should we hold people with no education to lower standards and accept and forgive if they commit crimes? Does it matter what your educational or financial worth is if we're talking about international criminal law? I suggest that it does not. It's woefully irrelevant to consider as an aggravating factor someone's education, someone's professional background. Secondly, unwillingness to assist certain individuals. It's absolutely, absolutely untrue that you can use that as a basis as an aggravating factor. First of all, the underlying premise by the Trial Chamber is -- I'm trying by best and I respect that -- is that there was an unwillingness by Dr. Stakic. The evidence is clear. He did not -- he did unwillingly -- strike that. The evidence is clear. He was not unwilling in his efforts. When Dr. Stakic was able to help, he did. When he was able to state things, he did. We found in the evidence that we produced that Dr. Stakic had three individual people close to his family exactly during the time of the indictment that asked him for some relief, two that went to the front, a nephew and a brother-in-law, who ultimately died in the front in former Yugoslavia. They asked him to see if he has any political power, and we have that in our brief to remove them from the military so they wouldn't go to the front. Dr. Stakic was unable to do that. Unwillingness and inability are two different things, and I suggest that in this case Dr. Stakic was never unwilling to assist. He was unable to assist. And more importantly, this is not an aggravating factor, whether he was willing or unwilling to assist an individual. He was convicted of crimes here. To compound the significance and prejudice of this I think is unfounded in the legal jurisprudence. We discuss quickly long phase of preparation, quickly on white-collar crimes. My comments are the same as it is with someone who has an education or a profession. We shouldn't raise or lower the standard depending on whether it is a blue-collar or a white-collar crime. They say also there was -- the crime of deportation, and I believe they haven't met the threshold. And from hearing my learned friend's comments on deportation, I'm convinced now that they haven't met the elements of deportation to even use it as a mitigating factor, much less to get a conviction on deportation. And finally with respect to superior position by Dr. Stakic, I think it's cumulative, it's duplicative, and I think it's multiplicative. Why? Because he was convicted in light of his position. He was not convicted for any personal conduct. They said because of your position or positions, we're convicting you. And now they come back at the end of the day and at the sentencing, say, that while your superior position, because of your superior position, we will now give you an aggravating factor and we will add to it. So they specifically enunciate that there are those six aggravating factors. I suggest, respectfully, that the Appeals Chamber reject each six. And I suggest the Appeals Chamber look at the issue of proportionality. It's a twofold concept, or multifold concept I suggest. One is proportionality with other sentences for other individuals in the same capacity roughly at the same time. With respect to Dr. Stakic, which we highlighted in our final brief, we say proportionality if you look at it as to who. If we examine the other cases, such as Celebici and Delalic, we should look for two critical things; that is, one, where former or members of the Crisis Staff or presidents of the Municipal Assembly, were they charged at all. In one case one was charged; in the other there were no charges. The witness who was the president of the Municipal Assembly and the witness who was the president of the Crisis Staff was not charged in the Konjic and in the Celebici case, which is the municipality there. He merely came as a witness, although at the same time the atrocities that were alleged happened there, he was president of that Crisis Staff, president of the Municipal Assembly. In Delalic, what happened when they ultimately or initially charged the president of the Municipal Assembly and the Crisis Staff? He was charged -- oh, that's on Lasva Valley, I'm sorry. You're right. Just quickly -- I know I'm pushing the limit and I apologise. If I can indulge two more minutes. In that case, if we compare on the principle of proportionality, if you compare in that case what happened to that individual who was ultimately charged, charges were dismissed before it got through a pre-trial stage of any significance. We believe that likewise Dr. Stakic in this case, the Trial Chamber should have dismissed it. But I humbly say to this trial court [sic] that not only were there multiple errors of fact that were a miscarriage of justice, but there were certainly discernible errors of law which require not only a full examination but a reconstitution of what the verdicts were in this case. We believe also separately that the sentence was enormously unparalleled with the proportionate sentences anywhere else in any other case for no other reason other than the Court misunderstood the law, misapplied the facts, and certainly, unnecessarily perhaps, misapplied all the aggravating factors. The Trial Chamber dismisses immediately any and all mitigating factors. We think our mitigating factors are actually quite strong, given that at that time Dr. Stakic was very young. We suggest to this Appeals Chamber to please, and I urge you with all my heart that you re-evaluate the enormous life sentence that was given to Dr. Stakic. I am telling you it is unfair given all the circumstances, and when you apply all the other elements of proportionality and the errors of law and fact that you'll find it in your hearts to reduce the sentence for this very young man. I also suggest that practice of finding the 20 years' minimum should be served with other contingencies is a violation of other treaties and agreements that the UN has with specific states. I outlined that in my brief. They don't address the issue. I'm sure they concede with that, and I believe that they also, the Trial Chamber took powers respectfully away from the President of the Tribunal in making decisions such as commutation of sentences, et cetera. It's outlined. I do want to say on behalf of Dr. Stakic and Mr. Lukic, I am very privileged to be here. I thank you very much for giving me the opportunity, and I apologise if we spoke too fast and too quick. And we ask this Court to take your time in the decision-making process, and we feel that if you examine the evidence consistent with the law that you will hopefully release Dr. Stakic from incarceration. Thank you, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your argument on behalf of the -- of Mr. Stakic. Now I would like to ask Mr. Stakic, as is customary, whether he would like to make a brief personal statement to the Court. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to address the Chamber a few sentences. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Of course. I invited you to do so. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] First of all, once again, thank you for allowing me to address you. Firstly, I would like to refer to the question put by His Honour to your right. I fear I might mispronounce His Honour's last name. I believe it was His Honour Guney. The question has to do with the statement of mine that was mentioned yesterday. I don't remember that I ever uttered such a statement, and if I uttered something similar it was phrased in different terms. However, that statement was contained in the newspaper article that was admitted here. And I would like to offer my deepest apologies to all of those who are offended by that statement. I would like to state that in the course of the trial there were more than ten witnesses who were either Muslims or Croats or Ukrainians, Germans, Poles. And if we had more time, we could have brought dozens of -- dozens more witnesses of diverse ethnic, religious background. I never discriminated against people on that basis. For me, the only division that can be made when it comes to different people are the evil and the good people. As for the events in the territory of Prijedor municipality, neither my defence nor I ever claimed that no crimes were committed there. However, the war did take place there. Who started the war is something that will be decided in future. The time will tell. The truth is that the crimes were committed, and I sincerely regret that anyone suffered and in any way became a victim of that war. However, I personally did not commit a single crime. I did not order a single crime, nor did I approve or justify a single crime either then or now. This is all I had to say. I do not wish to take up more of your time. Once again, thank you for allowing me to address you briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stakic. You may sit down. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The hearing of the appeal is now over, and I would like to thank the parties for their arguments, the interpreters, the registrar, and of course my distinguished colleagues for all the questions they have -- for all the questions and -- which they pursued with such great interest. But before we rise, I would like to raise another matter with Mr. Stakic. Mr. Stakic, you are due for a Status Conference with me in October. Now, you will recall that the relevant Rule allows any person in custody pending appeal the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the mental and physical condition of that person. You have of course the right to the Status Conference, as I mentioned before, but would you be interested in that conference or you would think that if you have any complaint you could perhaps voice it now and we would not need it? I let you decide on that. It's your right. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. When I addressed you just now, I did not raise several issues, the issues that I have mentioned previously. Namely, when I came here to the Detention Unit I was healthy. But for the past ten months I have been suffering from hypertension. This hypertension is not caused by physical factors but rather is psychosomatic. I now receive therapy. I tried to discontinue therapy for a week in agreement with my doctors. However, that aggravated my condition, and my blood pressure currently is 160/100, which is quite high for somebody of my age. Therefore, I went back to receiving my therapy. Other than that, I don't have other problems or complaints. And for these reasons, I think there is no need to schedule a Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I do hope - and the registrar could communicate it to the Detention Unit - that the condition that Mr. Stakic mentioned is taken good care of and that he's provided with good medical care. And I thank -- I understand that you do not insist on -- you do not ask for a Status Conference. I will construe that as waiving your right to that. So we will not meet again this month in the format of a Status Conference. I thank you for that. You may sit down. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And just one more issue. It was not my intention to complain to the conditions in the Detention Unit or to the medical care provided to me. No, I received a perfectly adequate therapy. However, what I wanted to say is that my condition has psychosomatic causes, and I had no intention of complaining against the doctors and the care I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I understand, Dr. Stakic, and I did not understand your comments as a complaint and I'm sure the registry did not either. I just wanted to make sure that you continued to receive good medical care. If there's -- there is no other comment you would like to make. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] I don't have other comments, and I hope that in the future things will be as they are now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stakic, and you may sit down. This concludes our hearing for today and the court stands adjourned.
